title: Stoicism
goal: Understand the Stoics' core ideas (virtue, what's in your control, emotions as judgments) and how they practiced them.

sections.headline: A former slave and an emperor followed the same philosophy.
sections.body: Epictetus had been enslaved. Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire. Both were Stoics, and both left writing you'll read in this lesson.

events.title: Zeno of Citium founds the school
Epictetus expelled from Rome
events.detail: A former slave, banished by Domitian along with other philosophers.

sections.heading: Philosophers of the porch
sections.body: The name comes from a place: the **stoa poikilê**, a porch in the Agora at Athens decorated with mural paintings, where Zeno taught. "Stoic" means, roughly, "porch person."

visual.accessibilityLabel: A simple colonnade: a roof on five columns, with paint and conversation symbols between them, for the painted porch where the Stoics taught.

sections.body: For the Stoics, only virtue benefits a person and makes a life go well. Health, wealth and reputation are "indifferents": some are naturally preferred, but none is good in itself.

sections.heading: What virtue looks like
sections.body: Virtue isn't one trait but a family of them. The Stoics named **prudence** (practical wisdom), **justice**, **courage** and **moderation**. They saw these as expressions of one good character, not separate skills.

visual.accessibilityLabel: Four virtues: prudence, justice, courage and moderation.

sections.heading: Two circles
sections.body: Epictetus's teaching starts with a sort. Some things are up to you: your opinions, aims, desires and aversions. Others aren't: your body, property, reputation and position. Peace comes from putting your effort only into the first circle.

visual.accessibilityLabel: Two circles. In your control: opinion, aim, desire, aversion. Not in your control: body, property, reputation, position.

sections.text: Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions.
sections.speaker: Epictetus

questions.prompt: According to Epictetus, which of these is in your control?
questions.explanation: Opinion, pursuit, desire and aversion are in our control; body, property and reputation are not.

questions.prompt: For the Stoics, wealth is good in itself, as long as you use it well.
questions.explanation: Wealth is an "indifferent": possibly preferred, but only virtue is good.

sections.text: Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.
sections.speaker: Epictetus

sections.heading: Emotions run on judgments
sections.body: The Stoics analyzed each harmful passion as a kind of judgment, often a false one, such as "this loss is terrible for me." Change the judgment and the passion changes. They weren't against feeling: they described good feelings that respond to things that are genuinely good.

visual.accessibilityLabel: An event, a friend cancelling, leads to a judgment, 'this is terrible', which produces a passion such as anger or distress.

sections.text: Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
sections.speaker: Marcus Aurelius

steps.title: Preview the day
steps.body: Marcus began mornings expecting difficult people: "I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."

steps.title: Sort by control
steps.body: Through the day, ask Epictetus's question: is this up to me? If not, let it go.

steps.title: Review the night
steps.body: Seneca described passing "the whole day in review" before sleep, asking: "What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day?"

sections.heading: Agreement with nature, citizens of one city
sections.body: The Stoic goal was **living in agreement with nature**, which includes our nature as rational, social beings. That led to a striking idea: all rational beings make up the citizenry of one universal city, a **cosmopolis**.

visual.accessibilityLabel: Widening circles of belonging: you, your city, and the cosmopolis of all rational beings.

sections.heading: Stoicism vs. "being stoic"

rows.label: Feelings
values: Harmful passions come from false judgments; good feelings are welcome

rows.label: Aim
values: Virtue, living in agreement with nature

sections.takeaway: The everyday word keeps the calm and drops the philosophy.

questions.prompt: What disturbs people, according to Enchiridion 5?
questions.explanation: "Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things."

questions.prompt: Seneca recommended reviewing your whole day each night.
questions.explanation: He described passing the whole day in review before sleep, asking what bad habit he had cured that day.

steps.title: Sort it
steps.body: The cancellation: not up to you. Your next move: up to you.

steps.title: Catch the judgment
steps.body: "This ruins everything" is an opinion, and opinions can be examined.

steps.title: Act on what's yours
steps.body: Rebook, call ahead, find food. Be decent to the gate agent: justice applies here too.

steps.title: Review it tonight
steps.body: What went well? What would you judge differently next time?

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Stoicism offers a working method rather than a mood: sort what you control, examine your judgments, act well, and review. Whether or not you accept every Stoic claim, those habits are easy to test in an ordinary week.

bullets: The Stoics held that only virtue (prudence, justice, courage, moderation) is truly good; health and wealth are "indifferents".
Some things are in our control (opinions, aims, desires) and many aren't; we're disturbed by our judgments, not by things.
Their practices are concrete: preview the day, sort by control, review the night.

finalQuiz.prompt: Where does the name "Stoic" come from?
choices: A painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught
finalQuiz.explanation: The name derives from the stoa poikilê, a porch in the Agora at Athens decorated with mural paintings.

finalQuiz.prompt: How did the Stoics understand harmful emotions (passions)?
finalQuiz.explanation: They analyzed each passion as a kind of judgment, so changing the judgment changes the passion.
Epictetus was a former slave; the Stoic emperor was Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 161 to 180 CE.

choices: The one universal city of all rational beings
finalQuiz.explanation: The Stoics held that all rational beings are citizens of one universal city.

finalQuiz.prompt: Being Stoic in the philosophical sense means suppressing all feelings.
finalQuiz.explanation: The Stoics targeted passions rooted in false judgments, and described good feelings that respond to genuine goods.
